extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theology, canon law, and church-state relations
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and historical rules about ecclesiastical authority: who may judge and pronounce sentences, the meaning and effects of excommunication, limits on councils and scripture becoming law, and the requirements for ecclesiastical offices in apostolic times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of judgment and sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly (the faithful) gives Judgment of the cause; the Apostle or some Pastor pronounceth the Sentence as Prolocutor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentence belonged always to the Apostle or some Pastor of the Church; the Assembly was first to hear the Cause and by consequence to condemn him. Example: St. Paul determined and pronounced the sentence (1 Cor. 5.3-5), while the Assembly judged the merit (1 Cor. 5.11-12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication (Aposunagogon Poiein) is to cast out of the Synagogue, i.e., out of the place of Divine service; the term is drawn from Jewish practice of casting out persons judged contagious in manners or doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to Jewish separation of lepers by the Law of Moses; originally meant exclusion from congregational worship rather than civil penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of excommunication without civil power
rubrics_metrics.description: While unstrengthened by civil power, excommunication's effect was limited to requiring the faithful to avoid the company of the excommunicate (not to eat with them), but it gave no civil exclusion from places unless the owner forbade it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Paul forbade keeping company with fornicators of the brethren (1 Cor. 5); excommunicate persons could not be compelled out of public places except by the civil magistrate or owner of the place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication has no effect upon apostates under civil persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Against a Christian who becomes an apostate in a place where civil power persecutes or does not assist the Church, excommunication had 'nothing in it'—no worldly damage nor terror, and in the world to come they were no worse than those who never believed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because apostates returned into the favour of the world, any temporal damage redounded rather to the Church (provoking persecutors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication affects only the faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication is effective only upon those who believe in Christ's coming to judge; it punishes by exclusion from the Kingdom of Christ as feared by the faithful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who truly believe fear the retention of sins; nonbelievers are not within the scope of this punishment since they do not expect Christ's kingdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper grounds for excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication lies for injustice and scandalous life (e.g., fornication, covetousness, idolatry, drunkenness, extortion) but not merely for difference of opinion that does not destroy the foundation that 'Jesus was the Christ.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural supports: Mat. 18 procedure for offences, 1 Cor. 5 list of scandalous behaviours. Doctrinal divergences preserving the foundation should not be cause for casting out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of heretics vs excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Apostle's advice to 'reject' a heretic (Titus 3:10) means to give over admonishing or set aside disputation, not to excommunicate; pastors should avoid making new binding articles for every small controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject/avoid (paraitou, periistaso) signals ceasing debate; examples: Timothy and Titus instructed to avoid foolish questions rather than excommunicate for them; Peter and Paul did not cast one another out despite controversy (Gal. 2.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons liable to excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a person who is a member of some lawful assembly (a Christian Church with power to judge) is subject to excommunication; where there is no community or power to judge, there can be no excommunication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One church cannot excommunicate another: either they are equal (in which case mutual excommunication is schism) or subordinate (then they are one church). The sentence presupposes a community that bound its members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits regarding sovereigns and civil obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication of a sovereign prince or assembly is of no effect on their subjects; subjects remain bound by natural law to be in the presence and company of their sovereign and cannot lawfully avoid or expel him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excommunication may have political effects (instigating war) but produces no obligation on subjects to disobey or refuse ordinary civil duties such as eating with the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication cannot extend beyond apostolic commission
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of excommunication is limited to the end for which apostles and pastors had their commission: teaching and direction toward salvation (correction of manners), not ruling by coercion or civil command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a master may abandon a negligent scholar but cannot accuse him of injustice for not obeying. The Church's authority is pastoral, not legislative in civil matters when unbacked by civil power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family relations and excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: If a parent or master be excommunicated, their children or servants are not forbidden to keep company with them or to eat with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbidding such company would often oblige children not to eat at all and would wrongly authorize disobedience to parents and masters contrary to apostolic precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreter of Scripture before Christian sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Before civil sovereigns became Christian, no single interpreter of Scripture had binding authority over converts; each hearer judged the force of scriptural arguments for himself, and apostles persuaded rather than commanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Paul's appeal to the Jewish Scriptures in Thessalonica required the listeners to judge his arguments; interpretation only becomes authoritatively binding when pastors also hold civil sovereign power.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Scripture becomes law
rubrics_metrics.description: A writing becomes 'canonicall' in the sense of law only where the lawful civil sovereign has made it so; otherwise scriptures are rules or counsel, not binding laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes canon as 'rule' from law as 'command of one we have given sovereign authority'; New Testament writings were counsel until civil power commanded obedience (e.g., when Christian sovereigns made them law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonicity of Old and New Testaments tied to civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Old Testament portions (e.g., Decalogue) were made law by Moses as civil sovereign; the Old Testament became commonly canonical when the covenant was renewed under Esdras and civil authority received them. The New Testament became law where Christian sovereigns or civil powers authorized it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Ten Commandments, Judicial and Levitical laws made canonical by Moses (who was civil sovereign); Old Testament translated and approved in Alexandria under civil authorities; New Testament received in practice by converts but became legally binding only when civil authorities commanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Councils' decrees are not legislative without civil backing
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of councils (including apostolic synods) are counsel/conditions proposed to converts, not universal laws, unless backed by civil sovereign authority; apostles' council acts obliged the apostles to teach but did not make everyone sin who refused them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts of the Council of the Apostles (Acts 15) used language 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you...' — interpreted as conditions for those seeking salvation rather than civil laws; councils cannot make new binding civil laws absent sovereign power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right and nature of ecclesiastical offices in apostolic time
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecclesiastical offices were magisterial (preaching, sacraments, teaching) and ministerial (deacons administering temporal needs). Apostles were the principal magisterial officers, chosen and constituted by Christ, with witnessing the Resurrection an essential mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apostles' office included preaching, baptizing, administering sacraments, teaching, and being martyrs (witnesses). The election of a new apostle (e.g., to replace Judas) required specific qualifications such as having seen Christ after the Resurrection or having conversed with him.
